words.definition: all the people who work for a company or are available to work in a country
words.example: Automation has reduced the size of the workforce needed on the factory floor.

words.definition: the amount of work that a person or machine has to do
words.example: Her workload doubled after two colleagues left the department.

words.definition: no longer employed because there is no more work for you, or not needed
words.example: Three hundred staff were made redundant when the factory closed.

words.definition: to encourage someone to do something by offering a reward
words.example: The firm incentivises punctuality with a small monthly bonus.

words.definition: to persuade someone to leave their job to work for another company
words.example: She was headhunted by a rival firm after only a year in the role.

words.definition: a state of extreme physical or emotional tiredness caused by prolonged stress
words.example: He took three months off work to recover from burnout.

words.definition: to control every small detail of someone's work rather than trusting them
words.example: Staff morale fell once the new director began to micromanage every decision.

words.definition: to give part of your work or responsibility to another person
words.example: Good managers learn to delegate tasks rather than trying to do everything themselves.

words.definition: to make a process simpler and more efficient
words.example: The new software streamlined the whole ordering process.

words.definition: working for different companies on particular pieces of work, rather than being employed
words.example: After leaving the agency, she became a freelance designer.

words.definition: an extra benefit given to someone because of their job
words.example: Free gym membership is one of the perks of working here.

words.definition: to do a second job, often secretly, in addition to your main one
words.example: He moonlights as a taxi driver at weekends to pay off his debts.

words.definition: all the subjects taught by a school, college or university
words.example: Cookery has recently been added to the school curriculum.

words.definition: learning by repeating something until you remember it, without necessarily understanding it
words.example: Critics argue that rote learning discourages students from thinking critically.

words.definition: the practice of using someone else's work or ideas without acknowledging them
words.example: The essay was rejected for plagiarism after software flagged copied passages.

words.definition: to supervise students during an exam to make sure no one cheats
words.example: Two teachers were asked to invigilate the final exam in the main hall.

words.definition: to give help and advice to a younger or less experienced person over a period of time
words.example: Senior staff are encouraged to mentor new graduates during their first year.

words.definition: to do less well than expected, especially in school work
words.example: Bright children sometimes underachieve simply because they are bored in class.

words.definition: the ability to read and write
words.example: The charity runs literacy programmes for adults who missed out on schooling.

words.definition: the ability to understand and work with numbers
words.example: Basic numeracy is tested alongside literacy in the entrance exam.

words.definition: relating to the skills and knowledge needed for a particular job
words.example: The college offers vocational courses in plumbing and electrical work.

words.definition: the world of teaching and research at universities and colleges
words.example: After years in industry, she returned to academia to finish her doctorate.

words.definition: someone who leaves school or college before finishing a course
words.example: The scheme was set up to support university dropouts back into education.

words.definition: money paid for teaching, especially at a university
words.example: Rising tuition fees have put many students off applying to university.

words.definition: the amount of carbon dioxide produced by a person's or organisation's activities
words.example: Flying less is one of the simplest ways to shrink your carbon footprint.

words.definition: the cutting down of trees in a large area
words.example: Deforestation in the region has accelerated sharply over the past decade.

words.definition: the number and variety of plants and animals living in a particular area
words.example: The wetland is prized for its exceptional biodiversity.

words.definition: energy from a source such as wind or sunlight that is not depleted when used
words.example: The country now generates over half its electricity from renewable energy.

words.definition: substances, especially gases, that are released into the air
words.example: The new regulations aim to cut emissions from heavy industry.

words.definition: the reduction in the amount of something, often a natural resource
words.example: Overfishing is a leading cause of the depletion of certain fish stocks.

words.definition: to balance the harmful effect of one thing with an equal and opposite effect
words.example: The airline lets passengers offset their flight's emissions by funding tree-planting.

words.definition: completely clean, fresh or unspoiled
words.example: Developers want to build a resort on one of the island's last pristine beaches.

words.definition: impossible to change back to a previous state
words.example: Scientists warn that some damage to coral reefs may already be irreversible.

words.definition: a gas, such as carbon dioxide, that traps heat in the atmosphere
words.example: Methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

words.definition: to use a resource so much that it becomes damaged or used up
words.example: Several fishing grounds have been overexploited to the point of collapse.

words.definition: all the living things in an area and the way they affect each other and the environment
words.example: Removing a single predator can disrupt an entire ecosystem.

words.definition: a set of rules followed by a computer to solve a problem
words.example: The app uses an algorithm to recommend songs based on your listening habits.

words.definition: the process of converting information into a code to prevent unauthorised access
words.example: The bank uses end-to-end encryption to protect customers' data.

words.definition: a small, usually temporary fault in a machine or system
words.example: A glitch in the booking system left hundreds of passengers without seats.

words.definition: software designed to damage or gain unauthorised access to a computer system
words.example: The hospital's network was taken offline after staff opened an email containing malware.

words.definition: permanent software programmed into a hardware device
words.example: The manufacturer released a firmware update to fix the battery problem.

words.definition: the way a computer program presents information to, and accepts instructions from, a user
words.example: The new interface is far more intuitive than the previous version.

words.definition: able to be made larger or smaller according to need
words.example: Investors were drawn to the start-up because its business model was highly scalable.

words.definition: an important discovery or development that happens after a lot of hard work
words.example: The lab announced a breakthrough in battery technology that could double range.

words.definition: to make a process or system operate using machines or computers instead of people
words.example: The warehouse has automated most of its sorting and packing.

words.definition: no longer used because something newer and better has been developed
words.example: The software made the old paper-based filing system completely obsolete.

words.definition: the most modern and advanced available
words.example: The hospital has invested in cutting-edge imaging technology.

words.definition: the amount of data that can be transmitted in a fixed time, or figuratively, mental capacity
words.example: The video kept freezing because the office's bandwidth couldn't cope with so many calls at once.

words.definition: describing an illness that lasts for a long time
words.example: He has suffered from chronic back pain since the accident.

words.definition: a sudden start of something unpleasant, especially a disease
words.example: An outbreak of food poisoning was traced back to a single restaurant.

words.definition: to wrongly identify the illness someone has
words.example: Her condition was misdiagnosed for years before a specialist finally identified it.

words.definition: a doctor's judgement about how a disease will develop
words.example: The prognosis improved considerably once the tumour was removed.

words.definition: involving a lot of sitting and little physical exercise
words.example: A sedentary lifestyle is linked to a higher risk of heart disease.

words.definition: the ability to recover quickly from illness or difficulty
words.example: The programme is designed to build emotional resilience in teenagers.

words.definition: a return of an illness after an apparent recovery
words.example: He suffered a relapse just weeks after finishing the treatment.

words.definition: a condition caused by not eating enough, or not eating enough of the right things
words.example: Malnutrition remains widespread in regions affected by the drought.

words.definition: considering the whole of something, including mental, social and physical factors
words.example: The clinic takes a holistic approach to treatment, looking beyond physical symptoms.

words.definition: the system in the body that fights disease and infection
words.example: A balanced diet helps keep the immune system functioning well.

words.definition: to make yourself too tired by trying too hard physically
words.example: He overexerted himself during the marathon and had to be treated for exhaustion.

words.definition: a period during which an illness, especially cancer, is less severe or appears to have gone
words.example: The disease has been in remission for almost two years now.

words.definition: a detailed plan of a journey
words.example: Our itinerary includes three nights in the mountains before heading to the coast.

words.definition: a short stop between two parts of a journey, especially by plane
words.example: We had a six-hour layover in Istanbul, so we left the airport to explore the city.

words.definition: the tired, confused feeling caused by travelling quickly across time zones
words.example: It took her almost a week to recover from the jet lag after the flight to Tokyo.

words.definition: away from places that are well known or often visited by tourists
words.example: If you want authentic food, head off the beaten track and avoid the main square.
collocations: a place off the beaten track

words.definition: a lot of busy and sometimes noisy activity
words.example: After the hustle and bustle of the city, the quiet village felt like another world.
collocations: the hustle and bustle of a city

words.definition: the feeling of confusion that people experience when they visit an unfamiliar culture
words.example: Moving to a country with such different customs gave her a real culture shock.

words.definition: moving from place to place rather than living in one place permanently
words.example: Some remote tourism projects are run in partnership with traditionally nomadic communities.

words.definition: to go somewhere that might be dangerous or unpleasant
words.example: Few tourists venture beyond the capital, which keeps the northern villages unspoiled.

words.definition: to start something new, especially something ambitious or difficult
words.example: They sold their house and embarked on a two-year trip around South America.

words.definition: quiet, private and away from other people
words.example: The resort is built around a secluded bay that is reachable only by boat.

words.definition: a short organised trip, usually for pleasure
words.example: The hotel offers a day excursion to the nearby waterfalls.

words.definition: a person who travels to many different countries
words.example: As a lifelong globetrotter, she has visited over eighty countries.

words.definition: a newspaper with small pages, short articles and often sensational stories
words.example: The story was splashed across the front page of every tabloid the next morning.

words.definition: the practice of banning parts of books, films or news from being seen or published
words.example: The documentary was pulled from the schedule amid accusations of censorship.

words.definition: biased or misleading information used to promote a particular point of view
words.example: Historians have studied how wartime propaganda shaped public opinion.

words.definition: an organisation, such as a television station or newspaper, that provides news to the public
words.example: Several news outlets ran the same story within hours of the leak.

words.definition: the presenting of stories in a shocking or exaggerated way to attract attention
words.example: Critics accused the channel of sensationalism rather than serious reporting.

words.definition: the quality of being believable or trustworthy
words.example: The newspaper's credibility suffered badly after the scandal.

words.definition: false information that is spread, whether deliberately or not
words.example: Platforms are under pressure to remove misinformation about vaccines more quickly.

words.definition: to become extremely popular very quickly online
words.example: Clips like this often go viral within hours of being posted.

words.definition: a strong negative reaction by a large number of people
words.example: The advert provoked such a backlash that the company withdrew it within a day.

words.definition: the reporting of news or events by newspapers, television, etc.
words.example: The election received extensive coverage across every major outlet.

words.definition: a particular, often biased, way of presenting information to influence opinion
words.example: Voters are growing tired of political spin and want straight answers.
collocations: put a positive spin on something

words.definition: online content designed mainly to attract attention and encourage clicks, rather than inform
words.example: The headline was pure clickbait and had almost nothing to do with the article.

words.definition: no longer close or friendly with someone, especially a family member
words.example: He had been estranged from his brother for almost a decade before they finally spoke again.

words.definition: a friendly relationship in which people understand each other well
words.example: The therapist quickly built up a good rapport with her young clients.

words.definition: to become friendly with someone again after a disagreement
words.example: The sisters finally reconciled after years of barely speaking.

words.definition: to tell someone a secret, trusting them not to tell anyone else
words.example: She confided in her closest friend about her plans to leave the company.

words.definition: a strong but usually short-lived feeling of love or attraction
words.example: Looking back, she realised it had been infatuation rather than real love.

words.definition: a feeling of friendship and the pleasure of being with someone
words.example: Many elderly residents say they value the companionship of the day centre most of all.

words.definition: to have an argument with someone and stop being friendly
words.example: The two business partners fall out with each other so often that staff barely notice anymore.

words.definition: to have a friendly relationship with someone
words.example: She has always managed to get on with her in-laws remarkably well.

words.definition: to resemble an older relative in appearance or character
words.example: Everyone says she takes after her grandmother, both in looks and temper.

words.definition: to gradually stop being close to someone over time
words.example: Old school friends sometimes grow apart simply because their lives go in different directions.

words.definition: a person with whom one has a strong affinity or bond
words.example: She describes her business partner as a creative soulmate rather than just a colleague.

words.definition: a strong dedication to someone or something, or a promise to do something
words.example: Moving in together was a sign of their growing commitment to one another.

words.definition: the official decision of a jury or judge on whether someone is guilty
words.example: The jury took less than two hours to reach a verdict.

words.definition: a formal statement given as evidence in a court of law
words.example: Her testimony proved crucial in securing the conviction.

words.definition: to officially charge someone with a crime and try to prove in court that they are guilty
words.example: The company was prosecuted for breaching safety regulations.

words.definition: to officially decide that someone is not guilty of a crime
words.example: He was acquitted of all charges after new evidence came to light.

words.definition: the process of taking legal action in court
words.example: The dispute between the two companies ended in years of costly litigation.

words.definition: a person who has been accused of a crime in a court of law
words.example: The defendant remained silent throughout most of the trial.

words.definition: the state of being kept in prison, or the legal right to care for a child
words.example: He was held in custody until his trial could be arranged.

words.definition: a period during which an offender is supervised in the community instead of being sent to prison
words.example: She was given twelve months' probation instead of a prison sentence.

words.definition: to discourage someone from doing something by making it seem difficult or unpleasant
words.example: Harsher penalties were introduced to deter repeat offenders.

words.definition: a minor crime or wrongdoing
words.example: What began as a minor misdemeanour quickly escalated into a serious charge.

words.definition: to interfere with something in order to change or damage it, often illegally
words.example: Someone had clearly tampered with the lock before the break-in.

words.definition: a person who brings a case against someone else in a court of law
words.example: The plaintiff argued that the company had failed to honour the contract.

words.definition: the money a person has left to spend after paying taxes and essential bills
words.example: As rents rise, young professionals are left with far less disposable income.

words.definition: to steal money that has been entrusted to you, especially from an employer
words.example: The former treasurer was accused of embezzling thousands of pounds from the charity.

words.definition: money given by a government to help an industry or activity continue
words.example: Farmers rely heavily on government subsidies to stay profitable.

words.definition: a sum of money that has to be paid, especially as a tax
words.example: A new levy on plastic packaging came into force this year.

words.definition: a situation in which a government spends less money, often leading to economic hardship
words.example: A decade of austerity left many public services badly underfunded.

words.definition: a general rise in prices across an economy over time
words.example: Inflation has pushed the price of basic groceries up sharply this year.

words.definition: an amount of money that someone receives unexpectedly
words.example: The unexpected windfall allowed them to pay off the rest of the mortgage early.

words.definition: to waste money, time or an opportunity carelessly
words.example: He squandered most of his inheritance on risky investments within a year.

words.definition: careful about spending money or using resources, avoiding waste
words.example: Growing up during the recession made her remarkably frugal with money.

words.definition: an arrangement allowing someone to take out more money from their bank account than it contains
words.example: She was charged a hefty fee for exceeding her overdraft limit.

words.definition: a thing of value owned by a person or company
words.example: Property remains the company's single biggest asset.

words.definition: a debt or financial obligation, or something that causes problems
words.example: The outstanding loans are listed as a liability on the balance sheet.

words.definition: an idea or explanation that is proposed and then tested through research
words.example: The team designed an experiment specifically to test their hypothesis.

words.definition: based on observation or experiment rather than theory alone
words.example: There is now strong empirical evidence linking the chemical to the disease.

words.definition: a connection or relationship between two things
words.example: Researchers found a clear correlation between sleep and academic performance.

words.definition: a factor that can change and that is measured or controlled in an experiment
words.example: The study controlled for several variables, including age and income.

words.definition: something that is unusual or does not fit the expected pattern
words.example: The unusual reading was dismissed at first as a simple anomaly.

words.definition: to repeat an experiment or study to see if the same results occur
words.example: Other laboratories have struggled to replicate the original findings.

words.definition: describing research that has been checked and approved by other experts before publication
words.example: The claim has not yet appeared in any peer-reviewed journal.

words.definition: a fact or situation that is observed to exist, especially one not fully understood
words.example: Scientists still cannot fully explain the phenomenon of ball lightning.

words.definition: to form an opinion or theory without firm evidence
words.example: Researchers can only speculate about what caused the sudden decline in the population.

words.definition: not leading to a definite result or decision
words.example: The trial results were inconclusive, so a larger study is now planned.

words.definition: thorough, careful and exact
words.example: The drug underwent rigorous testing before it was approved.

words.definition: introducing new ideas or methods for the first time
words.example: The groundbreaking study changed how scientists understood the ageing process.

words.definition: new and experimental, especially in art, music or literature
words.example: The gallery is known for championing avant-garde artists ignored by the mainstream.

words.definition: concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty
words.example: The building was praised for its aesthetic appeal as much as its function.

words.definition: a detailed analysis and assessment of something, especially a work of art
words.example: The professor's critique focused on the painting's unusual use of colour.

words.definition: to create or perform something without preparation
words.example: The actors had to improvise an entire scene after the script was lost.

words.definition: describing art that does not attempt to represent things realistically
words.example: Her early work was figurative, but she later moved towards abstract painting.

words.definition: to bring a feeling, memory or image into someone's mind
words.example: The soundtrack was designed to evoke a sense of nostalgia.

words.definition: to represent or describe someone or something in a work of art
words.example: The film portrays the city as both glamorous and dangerous.

words.definition: the use of humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise people or society
words.example: The novel is a biting satire on modern celebrity culture.

words.definition: confident, lively and noticeable, often in a colourful or dramatic way
words.example: The designer was known for his flamboyant costumes and theatrical shows.

words.definition: a particular material or method used by an artist
words.example: Watercolour has always been her preferred medium.

words.definition: to show a work of art or object publicly
words.example: Her photographs were exhibited at the national gallery last spring.

words.definition: an outstanding work of art or craftsmanship
words.example: Critics immediately hailed the film as a masterpiece.

words.definition: the part of the mind that affects behaviour without a person being fully aware of it
words.example: Advertisers often target the subconscious rather than conscious decision-making.

words.definition: relating to mental processes such as thinking, remembering and reasoning
words.example: The study examined the cognitive effects of long-term sleep deprivation.

words.definition: tending to examine one's own thoughts and feelings closely
words.example: Keeping a diary made her far more introspective about her choices.

words.definition: to find reasons to explain or justify your own behaviour, often unconvincingly
words.example: He tried to rationalise skipping the meeting by claiming it wasn't important anyway.

words.definition: to prevent yourself from expressing a feeling or desire, often unconsciously
words.example: She had repressed the memory for so long that it took years of therapy to surface again.

words.definition: the ability to understand and share the feelings of another person
words.example: Good counsellors show genuine empathy without becoming overwhelmed themselves.

words.definition: a refusal to accept that something unpleasant or painful is true
words.example: He remained in denial about the illness for months after the diagnosis.

words.definition: a strategy used to deal with stress or a difficult situation
words.example: Humour became her main coping mechanism during the difficult months after the move.

words.definition: confidence in your own worth or abilities
words.example: Constant criticism at work had slowly damaged his self-esteem.

words.definition: a systematic error in thinking that affects judgement and decisions
words.example: Confirmation bias is one of the most common forms of cognitive bias.

words.definition: existing in a person or animal from birth, not learned
words.example: Some researchers argue that a sense of fairness may be innate rather than taught.

words.definition: tending to act suddenly without thinking about the consequences
words.example: His impulsive decision to quit cost him a secure, well-paid job.

words.definition: all the people in a country or area who are entitled to vote
words.example: Nearly seventy per cent of the electorate turned out for the referendum.

words.definition: a complicated system of official rules and procedures, often seen as excessive
words.example: Small business owners complain constantly about bureaucracy slowing down every application.

words.definition: a temporary alliance between political parties, often to form a government
words.example: No single party won a majority, so a coalition government was formed.

words.definition: a vote in which everyone can take part on a particular political question
words.example: The government promised to hold a referendum on the proposed reform.

words.definition: divided into two sharply opposing groups with little middle ground
words.example: Public opinion on the policy has become increasingly polarised over the past year.

words.definition: relating to ordinary people rather than leaders, especially in politics
words.example: The campaign began as a small grassroots movement before gaining national attention.

words.definition: to try to persuade a politician or government to support or oppose something
words.example: Environmental groups have been lobbying hard for stricter emissions targets.

words.definition: an area whose voters elect a representative to a parliament or assembly
words.example: The new boundaries will merge two neighbouring constituencies into one.

words.definition: dishonest or illegal behaviour by people in positions of power
words.example: The minister resigned following allegations of corruption.

words.definition: the enforced separation of different groups of people, often by race
words.example: The museum documents the long struggle to end racial segregation.

words.definition: a system in which the government provides social and financial support to citizens
words.example: The country built one of Europe's most generous welfare states after the war.

words.definition: a law or set of laws passed by a parliament or similar body
words.example: New legislation requiring clearer food labelling comes into force next month.

words.definition: despite what has just been said; nevertheless
words.example: The journey was exhausting; nonetheless, she arrived in good spirits.

words.definition: used to add extra information to support a point already made
words.example: The plan is expensive; furthermore, it would take years to complete.

words.definition: used to introduce a contrast between two facts
words.example: City rents have risen sharply, whereas wages have barely moved.

words.definition: despite; in spite of (a formal word)
words.example: Notwithstanding the criticism, the project went ahead as planned.

words.definition: as a result of something just mentioned
words.example: The factory failed its safety inspection; consequently, production was halted.

words.definition: although; used to add a qualification to something already said
words.example: The team won the match, albeit by the narrowest of margins.

words.definition: to the extent that
words.example: The plan is sound insofar as it addresses the budget, but it ignores staffing.

words.definition: considering the fact that
words.example: Given that ticket sales were so low, the festival is unlikely to return next year.

words.definition: on condition that; only if
words.example: You can borrow the car provided that you fill it up with petrol afterwards.

words.definition: until now or until a particular time (formal)
words.example: The report revealed data that had hitherto been kept secret.

words.definition: in the middle of, or during (often used with difficult situations)
words.example: Share prices fell amid growing concerns about inflation.

words.definition: while waiting for something; until something happens
words.example: The licence has been suspended pending the outcome of the investigation.

words.definition: except for, or unless something happens
words.example: Barring any last-minute setbacks, the bridge should open by the end of the year.

words.definition: taking into account; considering
words.example: Given the circumstances, the committee agreed to extend the deadline.
